title: Enforcement and Sanctions
summary: A ten-module programme taking enforcement and supervisory staff through the full life of an enforcement case, from triage and evidence to sanctions, settlement and cooperation.
intro: This training programme equips supervisory authority staff to run fair, robust enforcement cases: deciding when to investigate, gathering evidence to an enforcement standard, determining proportionate sanctions, settling, and cooperating with prosecutors and other authorities.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To equip staff with the distinct skills enforcement demands over and above ongoing supervision: evidence-gathering to a legal standard, procedural fairness and sanctioning judgement. Participants leave able to take a case from referral to outcome in a way that is proportionate, consistent and able to withstand challenge.
sections.What It Covers: Enforcement powers and purpose, the decision to investigate and case triage, investigation planning, evidential standards and disclosure, chain of custody and digital evidence, investigative interviews and witness statements, procedural fairness, proportionate sanctions, settlement, criminal referral and cooperation, and tribunal and court proceedings.
Intended Audience: Enforcement investigators, case managers and lawyers
Supervisors who refer cases to enforcement or work alongside enforcement teams
Members of decision-making committees and senior staff responsible for sanctioning and settlement decisions
Learning Objectives: Explain the enforcement function, its powers and how it differs from supervisory intervention
Apply criteria and a triage framework to decide which cases to investigate
Gather, preserve and present evidence to a standard that will withstand legal challenge
Design and apply decision-making processes that meet procedural fairness standards
Determine proportionate, consistent sanctions and judge when settlement serves the public interest
Coordinate effectively with prosecutors and domestic and foreign authorities
sections.Structure and Format: Ten modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a multi-day programme or as a series of half-day sessions. Modules combine short input with case studies, evidence exercises and negotiation role-play, ending in an end-to-end case workshop, and can be selected or tailored to the authority's own powers and procedures.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some experience of supervision, investigations or regulatory legal work is helpful. No formal legal qualification is required.
Core Reading: IOSCO, Credible Deterrence in the Enforcement of Securities Regulation (2015)
IOSCO, Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation (2017)
IOSCO, Multilateral Memorandum of Understanding (MMoU) and Enhanced MMoU (2016)

modules.title: The Enforcement Function and Its Powers
modules.summary: The purpose of enforcement within the supervisory toolkit, the powers an authority typically holds, and why enforcement requires different skills and decision standards from ongoing supervision.
objectives: Explain the purposes of enforcement: deterrence, remediation and market confidence
Describe investigative, sanctioning and remedial powers
Distinguish enforcement from ongoing supervisory intervention
syllabus: Credible deterrence and the role of enforcement in the authority's strategy
Types of power: investigative, sanctioning, remedial and restitution
IOSCO principles for enforcement and international practice
Where supervision ends and enforcement begins

modules.title: Deciding to Investigate: Referral and Case Triage
modules.summary: How cases reach enforcement, the criteria for opening an investigation, and how triage directs limited resource to the cases with the greatest impact.
objectives: Describe referral routes from supervision and other sources into enforcement
Apply criteria for deciding whether to open an investigation
Prioritise a caseload using severity, evidential strength and public interest
syllabus: Referral sources: supervision, whistleblowers, complaints and other authorities
Statutory thresholds and the decision to investigate as a judgement
Triage: severity, harm, evidential strength and public interest
Exercise: triaging a set of sample referrals

modules.title: Planning and Managing an Investigation
modules.summary: How to scope and plan an investigation, resource it with the right skills, and manage a caseload so that cases progress without drift or backlog.
objectives: Scope an investigation with clear hypotheses and lines of enquiry
Plan resources, timelines and use of external support
Manage a growing or backlogged caseload
syllabus: Investigation plans: scope, hypotheses, lines of enquiry and milestones
Skills, time and external support: forensic accountants and experts
Case governance, progress review and decisions to discontinue
Managing caseload pressure and resource constraints

modules.title: Evidential Standards and Disclosure
modules.summary: The higher evidential bar that enforcement action requires, the types of evidence available, and the disclosure and privilege obligations that run throughout an investigation.
objectives: Explain the evidential standards for enforcement compared with supervisory action
Describe disclosure obligations to the subject of an investigation
Identify the limits that legal privilege places on evidence
syllabus: Standards of proof and why supervisory evidence is often insufficient
Documentary, testimonial, digital and expert evidence
Disclosure obligations: managed throughout, not at the end
Legal privilege and its limits

modules.title: Gathering and Preserving Evidence
modules.summary: Practical techniques for obtaining evidence using formal powers, preserving it without contamination and maintaining a chain of custody that will survive challenge.
objectives: Apply formal information-gathering powers appropriately
Maintain a defensible chain of custody and record of provenance
Identify evidence-handling errors that undermine cases
syllabus: Information requirements, document production and on-site visits
Preserving digital evidence: devices, communications and data
Chain of custody and documenting provenance
Exercise: finding the gaps in a sample evidence file

modules.title: Investigative Interviews and Witness Statements
modules.summary: How to conduct compelled and voluntary interviews to an enforcement standard and take witness statements that are accurate, fair and evidentially sound.
objectives: Plan and conduct interviews to an enforcement standard
Draft an evidentially sound witness statement
Avoid leading or suggestive questioning that weakens evidence
syllabus: Compelled versus voluntary interviews and the rights of interviewees
Interview planning, disclosure before interview and legal representation
Structuring a witness statement and avoiding suggestion
Case study: a case undermined by weak interview evidence

modules.title: Procedural Fairness in Enforcement Decisions
modules.summary: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' understanding of the principles of procedural fairness that must be applied in enforcement decision-making, including the right to make representations and managing conflicts of interest.
objectives: Explain the principles of natural justice as applied to enforcement
Describe the right to make representations and how it is given effect
Identify and manage conflicts of interest in enforcement decision-making
Assess whether a decision-making process meets procedural fairness standards
Formulate a fair process design for a sample enforcement case
syllabus: The two pillars of natural justice: right to be heard, freedom from bias
How natural justice applies specifically to enforcement decisions
Consequences of procedural unfairness for enforcement outcomes
International and domestic case law touchpoints
Facilitated discussion: procedural fairness challenges participants have encountered
Giving effect to the right to make representations
Timelines and format for representations
Identifying conflicts of interest in the decision-making chain
Structural separation between investigation and decision functions
Group exercise: identify conflicts of interest in a sample decision-making structure
Criteria for assessing procedural fairness of a process
Designing a fair process from the outset rather than retrofitting
Case study: a decision challenged on procedural fairness grounds
Case study: design a procedurally fair decision-making process for a sample case
Recap: natural justice, representations, conflicts of interest
Reflection and discussion
Q&A

modules.title: Determining Proportionate Sanctions
modules.summary: The aim of this workshop is to build participants' skills in applying a sanctioning framework consistently, weighing aggravating and mitigating factors and maintaining consistency with precedent while addressing the specific facts of a case.
objectives: Explain the purpose of sanctions within the enforcement toolkit
Apply a structured sanctioning framework to a case
Weigh aggravating and mitigating factors systematically
Assess consistency with precedent when determining a sanction
Formulate a proportionate sanction for a sample case
syllabus: Sanctions as deterrence, punishment, and market signalling
Types of sanction: financial penalties, restrictions, public censure
Proportionality as the guiding sanctioning principle
The role of published sanctioning guidelines
Facilitated discussion: sanctioning approaches from participants' own jurisdictions
Structured sanctioning frameworks: seriousness, harm, culpability
Aggravating factors: repeat conduct, concealment, senior involvement
Mitigating factors: self-reporting, remediation, cooperation
Financial penalty calculation methodologies
Group exercise: apply a sanctioning framework to a sample case
Using precedent to maintain sanctioning consistency
Distinguishing genuinely comparable cases from superficially similar ones
Case study: determining a sanction for a sample enforcement case
Case study: formulate a proportionate sanction, referencing precedent
Recap: purpose, framework, aggravating/mitigating factors, precedent
Reflection and discussion
Q&A

modules.title: Settlement and Negotiated Outcomes
modules.summary: The benefits and risks of settlement, when it is and is not appropriate, negotiation technique specific to enforcement, and the public interest test every settlement must meet.
objectives: Explain the rationale for settlement and common discount mechanisms
Assess when settlement should be pursued or resisted
Evaluate a proposed settlement against deterrence and the public interest
syllabus: Speed, certainty and resource efficiency versus perceived leniency
Settlement discounts, timing and transparency of settled cases
Negotiation technique and power dynamics between authority and firm
Role-play: negotiating a settlement

modules.title: Cooperation, Litigation and Seeing a Case Through
modules.summary: Brings the programme together: criminal referral and parallel proceedings, cooperation with domestic and foreign authorities, giving evidence before tribunals and courts, and feeding outcomes back into supervision.
objectives: Decide when criminal referral is appropriate and manage parallel proceedings
Use information-sharing gateways with prosecutors and domestic and foreign authorities
Prepare to give evidence and defend a decision before a tribunal or court
syllabus: Criminal referral, sequencing and the risk of prejudicing proceedings
Cooperation with police, tax authorities, the national FIU and foreign regulators
Giving evidence, appeals and publication of outcomes
Workshop: taking a case from referral to outcome

related.title: Conducting Regulatory Investigations: From Referral to Outcome
related.summary: An eight-module practitioner programme taking enforcement staff through a regulatory investigation, from referral and powers to compelled interviews, findings and outcome.

related.title: Asset Recovery: Tracing, Freezing and Confiscation
related.summary: An eight-module programme equipping practitioners to trace, restrain, confiscate, manage and return criminal assets, including crypto-assets and assets held abroad.

related.title: Authorisation and Licensing: The Regulatory Gateway
related.summary: A ten-module programme giving authorisation staff a structured, defensible methodology for assessing applications, key individuals, owners and changes at the regulatory gateway.

related.title: Crisis Management and Resolution
related.summary: A ten-module programme preparing supervisors for firm and system-wide stress, from early intervention and recovery and resolution planning to crisis communication and a live simulation.

related.title: Crypto-Asset Financial Crime: Typologies, Tracing and Controls
related.summary: An eight-module programme equipping supervisors, FIU analysts and investigators to recognise crypto-asset crime typologies, trace funds on-chain and assess service providers' controls.

related.title: Financial Crime Foundations for Regulatory Staff
related.summary: An eight-module foundation programme giving regulatory staff a grounding in AML/CFT, sanctions and fraud, firms' controls and financial crime red flags.
